title: ROCs in rats? Response to Wixted and Squire
central_proposition: The observation of linear Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) functions in rats performing recognition tasks is valid and consistent with dual-process models of recognition memory, contrary to critiques based on a single-process model.

concept_definitions.name: ROC functions (Receiver Operating Characteristics)
concept_definitions.definition: A plot of the probability of hits against the probability of false alarms across different response criteria, used to assess recognition memory performance.

concept_definitions.name: Single-process model (Unequal Variance Signal Detection Model)
concept_definitions.definition: A model of recognition memory that posits a single underlying memory strength dimension, typically predicting curvilinear ROCs.

concept_definitions.name: Dual-process model
concept_definitions.definition: A model of recognition memory that posits two distinct processes, familiarity and recollection, which contribute differently to recognition judgments and can predict both curvilinear and linear ROCs.

concept_definitions.name: Linear ROCs
concept_definitions.definition: ROC functions that appear linear when plotted in z-space (zROCs), often associated with recollection-based memory.

concept_definitions.name: Curvilinear ROCs
concept_definitions.definition: ROC functions that appear curved, often associated with familiarity-based memory.

concept_definitions.name: Payoff ratios
concept_definitions.definition: Experimental manipulation of the relative rewards or costs for correct and incorrect responses, used to induce different response biases and generate ROCs.

concept_definitions.name: d'
concept_definitions.definition: A measure of sensitivity or accuracy in signal detection theory, calculated based on the distance between signal and noise distributions.

concept_definitions.name: Percent correct
concept_definitions.definition: A simple measure of accuracy calculated as [P(hit) + (1 - P(FA))]/2 × 100.

concept_definitions.name: Differential outcomes effect
concept_definitions.definition: An effect where different outcomes are associated with correct responses to different stimuli, potentially influencing learning and performance.

argument_structure: The authors defend their empirical findings of linear ROCs in rats by directly refuting methodological and theoretical criticisms raised by Wixted and Squire. They argue that their methods (payoff ratios) are valid, their data's accuracy variation is acceptable, and their results are consistent with the dual-process model, which better explains the observed ROC shapes under varying memory demands than the single-process model.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism proposed is that different recognition memory demands (e.g., item vs. associative recognition, varying delays) selectively engage distinct underlying memory processes (familiarity and recollection). Familiarity is associated with curvilinear ROCs, while recollection is associated with linear ROCs. The experimental protocol, by varying these demands, reveals the contribution of these processes, leading to different ROC shapes.

findings.antecedent: Linear ROC functions observed in rats performing recognition tasks
findings.consequent: Validity of ROC data and consistency with dual-process memory models
findings.mechanism: The observed linear ROCs, particularly U-shaped zROCs, align with findings in human associative recognition, supporting a dual-process account where recollection contributes to linearity.
findings.quote: our approach has been different; we examined our data using both the single- and dual-process models and found that the dual-process model provided a better fit in both studies.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Fortin et al. 2004; Sauvage et al. 2008

findings.mechanism: U-shaped zROCs are a common empirical finding across various associative recognition tasks in humans, indicating that linear ROCs (in z-space) are not rare as claimed by critics.
findings.quote: our ROCs are in perfect agreement with the vast majority of the findings from associative recognition tests (59 conditions from 17 different studies) (Parks and Yonelinas 2007), wherein a large majority showed the U-shaped zROCs as seen in our studies.

findings.antecedent: Manipulation of payoff ratios in recognition tasks
findings.consequent: Validity as a method to obtain a range of response criteria for ROCs
findings.mechanism: Historical precedent in signal detection theory and expert consensus (Macmillan and Creelman, 1991) support payoff ratios as a valid method, particularly for evaluating theoretical assumptions, and they do not inherently produce linear ROCs.
findings.quote: the manipulation of payoff ratios is considered a valid way to obtain a range of response criteria to determine ROCs, and this method has been used since the beginning of signal detection analyses.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Tanner and Swets 1954; Macmillan and Creelman 1991

findings.antecedent: ROC data from rat recognition tasks (Fortin et al. 2004; Sauvage et al. 2008)
findings.consequent: Level of accuracy variation across bias conditions (measured by d' or percent correct)
findings.mechanism: When d' is calculated according to the single-process model, the variation in accuracy across bias levels in the authors' data is not significantly different from or is smaller than that in the critics' human data, refuting the 'equal accuracy' critique.
findings.quote: when we calculated d' according to their model, we found that the variations in accuracy across levels were not significantly different between our ROCs and theirs

findings.consequent: Explanation for linear ROC observations in rats
findings.mechanism: The differential outcomes effect, which involves distinct outcomes for correct responses to different stimuli, is not relevant to the authors' experimental design where reward contingencies are identical across conditions, thus it cannot explain the observed ROC shapes.
findings.quote: the differential outcomes effect is not relevant to our experiments and it is misleading to claim that it is.

findings.consequent: Shape of ROC functions (curvilinear vs. linear)
findings.mechanism: The same protocol yields curvilinear ROCs for item recognition at short delays (familiarity-driven) and linear ROCs for associative recognition at short delays or item recognition at longer delays (recollection-driven), demonstrating that the protocol itself does not force linearity but rather memory demands dictate the shape.
findings.quote: our protocol, explain why the ROC function of intact rats is linear under some memory demands and curvilinear under others, under the identical reward and effort contingencies.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Fortin et al. 2004; Sauvage et al. 2008

findings.antecedent: Memory demands (e.g., item vs. associative recognition, delay)
findings.consequent: Shape of ROC functions (linear vs. curvilinear)
findings.mechanism: The dual-process theory posits that familiarity contributes to curvilinear ROCs, while recollection contributes to linear ROCs. Different task demands selectively engage these processes, thereby determining the observed ROC shape.
findings.quote: different memory demands consistent with dual-process theory determine whether the ROC function is linear or curvilinear.

findings.antecedent: Rat recognition memory data (Fortin et al. 2004; Sauvage et al. 2008)
findings.consequent: Explanatory power of dual-process vs. single-process models
findings.mechanism: The authors' analyses in both studies found that the dual-process model provided a better fit to the observed ROC data, suggesting it more accurately captures the underlying memory processes.
findings.quote: we examined our data using both the single- and dual-process models and found that the dual-process model provided a better fit in both studies.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Fortin et al. 2004; Sauvage et al. 2008

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: ROC functions will be linear when memory demands primarily engage recollection (e.g., associative recognition, longer delays).
ROC functions will be curvilinear when memory demands primarily engage familiarity (e.g., item recognition, shorter delays).
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly connects observed ROC shapes to the predictions of the dual-process model of recognition memory, contrasting it with the single-process (Unequal Variance Signal Detection) model.
methodological_critiques: Critique of Wixted and Squire's assertion that linear ROC functions are rarely observed in humans, arguing their analysis focuses only on probability ROCs and ignores U-shaped zROCs which imply linearity.

Critique of Wixted and Squire's claim that the use of differential reward payoffs to manipulate response biases is unique and suspect, citing historical precedent and expert consensus for its validity.

Critique of Wixted and Squire's 'equal accuracy' requirement across bias levels as circular, noting it applies only within their single-process model and that accuracy naturally varies in both curvilinear and linear ROCs.
Critique of Wixted and Squire's explanation of linear ROCs via a 'differential outcomes effect', arguing it is not relevant to the authors' experimental design.
model_structure: The paper does not propose a new model but rather argues for the explanatory power and empirical support for the existing dual-process model of recognition memory over the single-process model, particularly in explaining the conditions under which linear vs. curvilinear ROCs are observed.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The paper evaluates the consistency and validity of linear ROC functions observed in rats performing recognition tasks with the predictions and interpretations of dual-process memory models.

The paper assumes Signal Detection Theory as the fundamental theoretical framework for the analysis and interpretation of Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves in memory research, which is central to its discussion of ROCs in rats.
